answers.primary: A skill exposed as a single slash command owns the pass: its instructions fan the roughly 400 route handler files out to read-only auditor subagents in bounded batches, and every finding must pass through a separate adversarial verifier subagent before it is written into the quarterly report.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow (a headless claude -p orchestration script); it also reruns from one command, but it adds external scripting and state plumbing that the in-session skill plus subagent fan-out does not need.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. A skill is advisory instruction text; the harness loads it, but nothing forces the model to visit all 400 files or to verify before reporting.
answers.context_boundary: Each auditor subagent runs in its own fresh context holding only its assigned files; only structured findings cross back to the orchestrating session, and verifier subagents likewise return only a confirmed or rejected verdict.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the user invokes the slash command each quarter; it ends when the report is written, and the skill file persists in the repo so next quarter's run is identical.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: under context pressure the model can shrink batches, skip files, or report unverified findings, and nothing in the harness blocks that; a per-file manifest with checkoff is the usual mitigation.
answers.version_caveat: Skills and subagents are stable features with no enabling flag; I recall the parallel subagent concurrency cap being around 10 with the rest queued, but I am not certain of the exact number.

answers.primary: An agent team of five teammates, one per hypothesis, using inter-teammate messaging to attack each other's theories, with the lead writing whatever consensus survives to the findings doc.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents; each can own a hypothesis but they cannot see or rebut each other's work, since subagent contexts never touch and results only meet in the caller after the fact.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model: the debating, disproving, and converging behavior is entirely prompt-driven, and nothing in the harness enforces genuine adversarial testing.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate holds a full separate context window; what crosses between them is explicit messages and the shared task list, and the findings doc on disk is the durable meeting point.
answers.lifecycle: The team is spawned for this one investigation and applies until it is disbanded or the session ends; the findings doc outlives the team.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: teammates may converge politely instead of disproving, sit idle waiting on messages, or burn large token volumes; a coordination failure loses the debate, not the data already written to the doc.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are an experimental feature gated behind an opt-in setting or environment flag; I do not remember the exact flag name and will not guess it.

answers.primary: A subagent (a custom test-runner agent definition) that executes the suite inside its own context and returns only the failing tests with their error messages; the tens of thousands of output lines live and die in the subagent's transcript.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill telling the main session to pipe test output through a filter script; it reduces noise but the raw stream still risks entering the working conversation whenever the filter or the model slips.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness enforces the isolation, because a subagent transcript is never merged into the caller's context, while the model owns whether the final report stays terse.
answers.context_boundary: The suite output exists only in the subagent's context; the single thing that crosses the boundary is the subagent's final report of failures and error messages.
answers.lifecycle: Dispatched on demand whenever the suite should run; the subagent's context is discarded as soon as its report returns.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the report edge: nothing caps the subagent's final message, so a sloppy agent can paste large log excerpts into its report and defeat the purpose; the agent definition should hard-limit the report shape.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents dispatched via the Task mechanism are stable with no enabling flag; agent definitions live in .claude/agents with YAML frontmatter controlling tools and model.

answers.primary: An agent team with three teammates owning the frontend, the backend API, and the test suite; teammates message each other as the interface contract shifts, and the user can address any teammate directly to redirect it without an intermediary.
answers.rejected_alternative: Three subagents; they satisfy the ownership split but fail both hard requirements, since subagents cannot message peers and the user cannot drop into a running subagent mid-flight.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model: contract synchronization happens only if teammates actually send updates, which is prompted behavior, not harness-checked.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate keeps its own context; contract changes cross as teammate messages and shared task list updates, and user redirections go straight into the targeted teammate's context.
answers.lifecycle: The team lives for the duration of the feature and stops applying when disbanded; nothing persists to future sessions except the code and any notes written to disk.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: silent contract drift when a teammate forgets to broadcast a change, and edit collisions if two teammates touch the same file since there is no file locking; experimental status adds general instability.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and gated behind an opt-in flag whose exact name I am not certain of; direct per-teammate user interaction is part of that experimental surface.

answers.primary: A Stop hook: when the model tries to end the turn, the hook itself runs the strict type check; on remaining errors it blocks the stop and feeds the error list back so the model fixes and retries, and it tracks the error count in a small state file so it allows the stop after a clean pass or after two consecutive rounds with no reduction.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that says loop until clean; that depends on the model choosing to keep looping, which is exactly the babysitting-by-hope this scenario forbids.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness: the hook executes deterministically outside the model, and its block decision is applied whether or not the model agrees.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs as an external process; only its block reason (the fresh type errors) enters the conversation, and its progress state lives in a file outside any context window.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every Stop event while configured in the project settings; it stops applying when the check passes, when the stagnation counter trips, or when the hook is removed from settings.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed by design, since the turn cannot end with errors outstanding; the key risk is a livelock if the progress detection is buggy, and conversely a crashing hook that exits with a non-blocking code fails open and silently lets the turn end.
answers.version_caveat: Stop hooks with block semantics (exit code 2 or a block decision in JSON output) are standard current hook behavior to my knowledge, with no enabling flag; hook configuration changes generally need a settings reload or new session and are reviewable via /hooks.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: an orchestration script (Agent SDK or headless claude -p) launched from one command, running a fixed-size pool of workers, each worker applying the identical transform inside its own git worktree, with a verifier step checking each result before the file is marked done in a state ledger.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team; teammates are built for collaborative, communicating work, and 500 identical independent transforms need throughput, isolation, and bookkeeping rather than discussion.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness side (the workflow script) owns sequencing, worktree isolation, retries, and the done ledger; the model owns only the quality of each individual transform.
answers.context_boundary: Every file's transform runs in a fresh headless session containing just that file's work; only pass or fail status and the diff cross into the shared ledger, and no long-lived conversation accumulates across the 500 files.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the command launches the script and ends when the ledger shows every file verified; reruns resume from the ledger instead of starting over.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed per file, because an unverified file stays not-done and gets retried; the realistic failures are integration-time worktree merge conflicts and gradual transform drift between isolated sessions.
answers.version_caveat: Headless claude -p and the Agent SDK are stable, and worktree isolation is plain git; I am not aware of a flag gate here, but I cannot quote exact SDK option names from memory.

answers.primary: Parallel subagents: one read-only reviewer subagent per changed file, dispatched in batches from the orchestrating session, which then merges, dedupes, and ranks the returned findings into a single summary.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team; the reviewers explicitly have nothing to discuss, so paying for teammate messaging and coordination buys nothing over a plain fan-out and merge.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model: batch discipline, covering all 60 files, and honest deduplication are all instruction-following, not harness-checked.
answers.context_boundary: Each reviewer sees only its own file's diff plus minimal PR context in a fresh subagent context; only structured findings return, and the merge and ranking happen in the caller's context.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the review is invoked, typically wrapped in a skill for repeatability, and ends when the merged summary is produced; nothing persists between runs.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: the concurrency cap forces batching so late batches can degrade, severity scales drift across independent reviewers which makes the ranking noisy, and one verbose reviewer can bloat the merging context.
answers.version_caveat: Subagent fan-out is stable with no enabling flag; I recall the parallel execution cap being about 10 concurrent tasks with the remainder queued, though I am not certain of the exact number.

answers.primary: A skill that runs a strict three-stage subagent pipeline: a finder subagent produces a findings report, a fixer subagent receives exactly that report and makes the edits, and a verifier subagent receives the report plus the diff and confirms; the skill text forbids reordering or blending stages.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team of three specialists; teams shine when peers work concurrently and talk, while this is a serial pipeline over the same handful of hot files where concurrency would cause edit collisions.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model: the orchestrating session enforces the sequence only as faithfully as it follows the skill, and nothing in the harness makes stage two wait for stage one.
answers.context_boundary: Each specialist runs in a fresh subagent context; the previous stage's report is injected into the next stage's prompt, so the handoff artifact is the entire interface and the main context carries only those reports.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by invoking the skill; each stage starts when the previous one returns, and the run ends at the verifier's verdict.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: the classic break is the lossy handoff, where the finder's report omits context the fixer needs, or the fixer's edits shift line numbers the verifier trusts; the orchestrator can also blur stages together.
answers.version_caveat: Skills and sequential subagent dispatch are stable, unflagged features; passing handoff artifacts by file path rather than inline text avoids output-size truncation limits whose exact values I cannot quote precisely.

answers.primary: An agent team with three teammates covering user experience, technical architecture, and a devil's advocate, debating through teammate messages as their positions form, with the user free to jump into any explorer and redirect it mid-flight.
answers.rejected_alternative: Three parallel subagents with an orchestrator synthesis; that produces three static essays instead of a reactive debate, and the user cannot steer an individual subagent once it is dispatched.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model: whether the perspectives genuinely engage each other's arguments is prompt-shaped behavior with no harness check.
answers.context_boundary: Each explorer keeps its own context; arguments cross only as explicit messages, and user redirections enter the chosen teammate's context directly rather than through the lead.
answers.lifecycle: The team exists for the exploration and stops at disband or session end; the surviving design rationale should be written to a file because team context is not durable.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: the devil's advocate can soften into agreement, message traffic can swamp actual thinking, and an experimental feature can drop or misroute messages; there is no deliverable unless someone is explicitly told to compile one.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and require an explicit opt-in flag or setting; I am not confident of the exact flag name and decline to invent it.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: one command starts a fresh headless orchestrator session (claude -p or the Agent SDK) that performs the review pass, dispatches an independent verifier subagent per finding, and emits exactly one verified summary; all per-finding verification chatter stays inside that separate session tree.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running the fan-out from my own session as nested subagents; to my recollection subagents cannot dispatch subagents of their own because the Task capability is withheld inside them, so verifier dispatches and results would have to flow through my conversation.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness guarantees the isolation, since a separate process's contexts can never leak into mine; the model owns whether the verifiers genuinely and independently check each finding.
answers.context_boundary: The review and all verification occupy the headless session and its subagent contexts; the only thing that crosses back is the single final summary, ideally as a file plus a short stdout verdict.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the wrapping command is invoked after changes land, and the process exits once the summary is emitted; nothing persists between runs except the summary artifact.
answers.failure_mode: Quality fails open, since verifiers can rubber-stamp findings rather than independently reproduce them, while delivery fails closed: if the headless run dies you get no summary at all, so the wrapper must check the exit status.
answers.version_caveat: Headless mode and the Agent SDK are stable and unflagged; the rule that subagents cannot spawn further subagents matches my knowledge of Claude Code, but I cannot cite the version where it is documented.
